Scale bar, 20 µm. c , Equivalent circuit diagram describing the interface between the cell-attached pipette before (i) and after (ii) tile insertion. Upon insertion, the recorded pipette voltage ( V p ) will change from an extracellular capacitive-filtered waveform to a linearly scaled one (quasi-intracellular recording). d , Numerical simulation of steady-state cell-attached (blue) and whole-cell (red) voltages as a function of pore resistance. R seal = 75 MΩ, C m = 60 pF, R m = 55.6 MΩ. e , Evolution of voltage recordings from the whole-cell and cell-attached electrodes during the tile insertion. f , (i) No change in neuron input resistance (left) and intracellular Ca 2+ level (right) before (black) and after (red) tile insertion (two-sided paired-sample t -test, R in , n = 11 neurons; Ca 2+ level, n = 9 neurons). (ii) Similar pore resistance revealed by DNA tiles with (red) and without (black) functional cholesterol tags upon neuronal membrane insertion (two-sided Mann–Whitney–Wilcoxon test, n = 9 neurons with cholesterol, 7 neurons without cholesterol). g , Schematic outlining the possible mechanism facilitating tile insertion in which adhesion force between the membrane-glass interface and lipids helps drive DNA tile insertion, including without cholesterol tags. h , The tile insertion time decreases with increased seal resistance ( n = 23 neurons, F (1) = 5.95, one-way ANOVA). i , Cholesterol tags speed up tile insertion (Mann–Whitney–Wilcoxon test, n = 9 neurons with cholesterol, 5 neurons without cholesterol). ### Quasi-intracellular access through DNA tiles
DNA tiles that form nanopore-like access across neuronal membranes should, in principle, support the same recording modes as nanoelectrode interfaces, including quasi-intracellular recordings analogous to nanopipettes 16 (Fig. 4a ). Numerical simulations supported this idea: as pore resistance decreased, the action potential (AP) recorded through the tile–membrane interface transitioned from a capacitively filtered extracellular waveform to a scaled intracellular waveform with increased amplitude (Supplementary Fig. 17 and Supplementary Note 2 ).

Right: a DC shift and a one-to-one correspondence to the intracellular spikes after about 10 min when DNA tiles self-inserted into the membrane. Insets show the AP waveform recorded from the cell-attached pipette at two time points. Scale bar, left, 5 ms, 0.1 mV; right, 5 ms, 5 mV. c , AP amplitude measured from the cell-attached pipette before ( t = 0; black) and after ( t = 10–20 min; red) tile insertion under loose-seal (left, R seal &lt; 0.3 GΩ) and tight-seal (right, R seal &gt; 1 GΩ) configuration (loose seal, n = 6 neurons; tight seal, n = 5 neurons, paired-sample t -test). The centre and the bounds of the box plots represent 50%, 25% and 75% percentiles, and the whiskers represent 1.5 interquartile range below/above the first or the third quartile. d , DNA tiles facilitate stable repeatable cell-attached quasi-intracellular measures. Top: the dual-pipette configuration. Middle: whole-cell intracellular recording (red). Bottom: cell-attached recording (black). (i) Initial loose-seal configuration with the cell-attached pipette just brought in contact with the whole-cell patched neuron, evident by the capacitive AP waveforms. (ii) Insertion of tiles reveals ohmic quasi-intracellular recordings. (iii) The cell-attached pipette is retracted, signalling a loss in quasi-intracellular recordings. (iv) After ~5–10 min, the cell-attached pipette is brought back in contact with the same patch of cell membrane populated with tiles. Note the near-immediate reflection of spikes. (v) Within a minute of reattaching the quasi-intracellular waveforms emerge.

### DNA tiles enable quasi-intracellular recordings in dendrites
Quasi-intracellular strategies offer a promising route to stable, higher-throughput access to local intracellular activity 8 , 52 . To test whether DNA tiles can provide such access in dendrites, we adapted the dual-pipette configuration from Figs. 3 and 4 : one pipette established whole-cell recording at the soma, while a second, tile-loaded pipette formed a cell-attached configuration on the apical dendritic trunk of L5 pyramidal neurons ( Methods and Fig. 5a ).

### Conclusion
In summary, we explored the electrical interface between DNA tiles and live neurons. We show that DNA tiles self-insert to form membrane-spanning channels, exhibit stochastic transport reminiscent of biological ion channel gating, enable ionic transport and permit small-molecule permeability (Figs. 1 and 2 ). This access increases neuronal passive conductance without affecting membrane resistance. In our configuration, the tiles add ~2 nS of conductance, a small, non-cytotoxic leak.
Structurally, the DNA tiles resemble previous designs 37 , composed of 11 nm DNA duplexes with a 0.8 nm central cavity, allowing compact yet functional lipid membrane interfacing. Negatively charged, hydrophilic DNA strands typically show poor neuronal uptake 53 , 54 , which limits membrane-spanning applications 55 . Hydrophobic modification is a standard solution to improve membrane anchoring 23 , 29 , 56 , 57 . Cholesterol tags markedly enhance membrane adhesion 58 , accelerating tile insertion into cortical neurons, as confirmed by insertion kinetics compared with unmodified tiles (Fig. 3 ). In addition, our data suggest an alternative insertion mechanism for untagged DNA nanostructures. The link between seal resistance and insertion suggests the mechanical force on membranes to be a possible promoter of tile embedding 47 .
Such engineered probes could serve as artificial membrane components and can be fabricated with controlled dimensions for targeting specific cellular or subcellular regions 25 , 59 . Recordings across tiles show stable conductance shifts and minor resistance changes, potentially useful for conditions where high resistance drives hyperexcitability. Leak conductances critically shape neuronal signalling, including excitability, signal integration, axial filtering and network synchronization 60 – 63 , and vary with inhibition, brain state and disease 64 , 65 . Thus, engineered passive leak channels could modulate excitability drug-free 66 . In addition, DNA structures

### DNA tile insertion and electrophysiological recordings
To maintain the physiological activities of the neuron, the tile insertion, incubation and recording were all performed at 34 °C ACSF under a constant carbogen supply. Borosilicate glass pipettes (4–7 MΩ) were pulled with a pipette puller (Sutter P1000) for the whole-cell and cell-attached recording. On the day of the experiment, freshly annealed DNA tiles (1 µM in buffer solution, 10 mM Tris-HCl, 1 mM EDTA, 20 mM MgCl 2 , pH 8.0) were diluted into 50–100 nM with ACSF (125 NaCl, 2.5 KCl, 1.25 NaH 2 PO 4 , 25 NaHCO 3 , 10 glucose, 2 MgCl 2 , 2 CaCl 2 , pH 7.4, osmolarity 300–310 mOsm) and the osmolarity was balanced with sucrose (&lt;5 mM) when necessary. In some experiments, 25 µM Alexa 594 or 100 μM Alexa 488 was added to the DNA tile suspension for visualization and verification that the membrane was not ruptured. The whole-cell patch-clamp pipette was filled with internal solutions containing (in mM) 130 potassium gluconate, 7 KCl, 10 HEPES, 5 NaCl, 35 sucrose, 2 MgSO 4 , 2 sodium pyruvate, 4 Mg-ATP, 0.4 Tris GTP, 7 phosphocreatine disodium, 0.025 Alexa 594 or 0.2 Alexa 488 (pH 7.3, osmolarity 290–300 mOsm). In some experiments, 200 µM fluo4 was added to the internal solution to monitor the intracellular Ca 2+ level. L5 pyramidal neurons were randomly assigned to treatment conditions (DNA tiles and control buffer). Both groups were tested within the same brain slices and brain regions to minimize confounds induced by variability in cell health or brain slice quality.
The neurons were visualized under an infrared (IR) Dodt contrast enhancement and an IR camera (Dage-MTI, IR2000) with a 40× objective (Nikon, 0.8 NA). The whole-cell recording was first formed to measure the baseline electrical properties (baseline RMP and so on). Neurons with access resistance larger than 30 MΩ or leak current larger than 300 pA (at −75 mV voltage clamp) were discarded. A small positive pressure (~0.5 psi) was maintained at the DNA tile-carrying pipette before contacting the neurona

### Preparation of giant vesicles
GUVs were prepared using an inverted emulsion method 78 . In brief, 1,2-dimyristoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (DMPC) and biotinylated lipids were mixed at a 1,000:1 molar ratio in chloroform in a glass vial. The solvent was evaporated under vacuum for 30 min to form a dry lipid film, which was subsequently resuspended in 600 μl of mineral oil and sealed with Parafilm. The oil–lipid suspension was sonicated at 50 °C for approximately 3 h to ensure homogeneous lipid dispersion.
Aqueous droplets were generated by adding 20 μl of Tris buffer (40 mM Tris, 1 mM EDTA, 20 mM acetic acid, pH 8.0) to the oil–lipid mixture, followed by vortexing for 30 s to produce a cloudy emulsion consisting of lipid-coated water droplets. A total of 600 μl of the emulsion was gently layered onto 300 μl of the same Tris buffer to establish an oil–water interface. The sample was centrifuged at 8,000 × g for 15 min, during which monolayer-coated droplets crossed the interface and assembled into bilayered GUVs that accumulated in the aqueous phase. After centrifugation, the mineral oil supernatant was carefully removed, and the GUVs were collected from the buffer phase.

### Microfluidic channel assembly
Microfluidic channels were fabricated by sealing a thin glass coverslip to a quartz slide using medical-grade acrylic double-sided adhesive tape. The channel geometry was defined by patterned slots cut into the adhesive layer. Before assembly, the glass coverslip was treated with piranha solution (H 2 SO 4 (3%):H 2 O 2 (1%)) to render the surface hydrophilic.

### GUV imaging
GUVs were imaged using a custom-built inverted fluorescence microscope based on a Zeiss Axio Observer D1 platform. Excitation was provided by diode lasers at 561 nm and 658 nm (Laserglow Technologies). Fluorescence emission was collected through a 63× oil-immersion objective (Zeiss) and detected with an Andor iXon3 electron-multiplying charge-coupled device camera.

### Abstract
Transmembrane ionic flow through artificial ion channels is integral to the development of biohybrid electronics, such as neural interface technologies. However, achieving accurate and stable intracellular access through these synthetic analogues has remained a challenge. Here we use DNA origami tiles (0.8 nm diameter), anchored into live neuronal membranes, both with and without cholesterol tags, to demonstrate highly stable ion transport (net ~2 nS), channel-like stochasticity and intracellular drug delivery without disrupting neuronal physiology. These results are supported by molecular dynamics simulations. Using a suite of patch-clamp techniques, including two-photon-targeted variants, we obtain repeatable intracellular and quasi-intracellular voltage measurements across DNA tiles, eliminating the need for membrane break-in even from thin dendritic structures (~1 µm), which are inaccessible with standard electrodes. This advancement establishes an ‘outside looking in’ method to probe intracellular voltage dynamics using DNA nanostructure-based transmembrane access.
Subject terms: Nanostructures, Characterization and analytical techniques, Drug delivery

### Main
Precise measurement of ionic flow across cellular membranes is fundamental when assaying bioelectricity in intact cells 1 . Traditional methods, such as whole-cell patch-clamp techniques 2 , offer invaluable insights into cellular dynamics but face major limitations, particularly when accessing smaller, more complex cellular structures or achieving stable intracellular measurements without disrupting integrity 3 . Recent bioengineering advances aim to overcome these challenges through innovations such as genetically encoded light and voltage-sensitive reporters 4 , synthetic analogues of ion channels such as carbon tiles 5 , 6 , and novel nanostructures 7 . However, achieving stable, repeatable electrical recordings with these tools remains difficult.
Artificial nanostructures—such as nanopipettes 8 , carbon nanotubes 5 , 9 , three-dimensional (3D) nanoelectrodes 10 – 12 and nanowires 13 , 14 —show promise as minimally invasive intracellular interfaces for neuronal recording 15 . Unlike traditional electrodes that often cause tissue damage, these nanoelectrodes minimally penetrate membranes, detecting subthreshold potentials, action potentials and previously inaccessible synaptic activity 16 – 19 . Yet intracellular recording still requires membrane rupture, which can disrupt physiology. Surface modifications and newer approaches to membrane access may help mitigate this issue 20 . Thus, novel nanostructures capable of self-insertion and lipid bilayer remodelling are needed to achieve seamless electrical access. Neurons rely on transmembrane ion flow for signalling 21 , and synthetically replicating this through artificial channels requires lipid bilayer membrane remodelling 22 . A promising approach uses artificial DNA tiles 23 , offering a platform for mimicking natural ion channel function. These biocompatible, ion-permissive nanostructures 24 – 26 enable transmembrane ionic transport, biosensing and membrane alteration 27 , 28 . Further modifications with hydrop

### DNA tiles enable ionic current measurements across neuronal membranes
The DNA tile assemblies feature tunable length 41 and channel size 42 , 43 . As previously reported 37 , each tile comprises 11-nm-long DNA duplexes with a 0.8 nm central cavity (Fig. 1a ). Eight single strands assemble into four duplexes; two include cholesterol molecules to facilitate membrane interfacing and two carry Cy3 or Alexa 488 for two-photon imaging. DNA sequences and chemical modifications are listed in Supplementary Table 1 , and their alignment with two-dimensional (2D) duplex maps is shown in Supplementary Fig. 1 .

### DNA tiles enable molecular delivery across neuronal membranes
Using dual-patch current-clamp recordings, we demonstrate that embedded DNA tiles enable intracellular delivery of small molecules, confirming transmembrane transport (Fig. 2 ). To validate this, we tested the transfer of a water-soluble, membrane-impermeable Alexa Fluor dye (~500 g mol −1 , negatively charged). Compared with capped tiles and control buffer, DNA tiles facilitated dye entry into neurons (Supplementary Fig. 10 ), confirming targeted molecular transport across membrane-anchored tiles.

### Characterization of pore resistance in neuronal membranes
The voltage-clamp recordings in Fig. 1 established DNA tile insertion into neuronal membranes via conductance changes but did not allow precise estimation of pore resistance owing to circuit constraints (Supplementary Note 1 ). To refine these measurements, we used a dual-pipette configuration ( Methods and Fig. 3a ). Two-photon imaging confirmed that tiles remained confined to the membrane patch in the cell-attached pipette, with no fluorescence wash-in, indicating that membrane integrity was preserved (Fig. 3b ). We analytically solved the equivalent circuit of the dual recording before and after tile insertion (Fig. 3c and Supplementary Fig. 13a ). Before insertion, the pipette voltage ( V p ) was dominated by the membrane capacitance (Fig. 3c(i) ), acting as a high-pass filter of the membrane voltage ( V m ) 46 . Upon tile insertion, ion permeability introduced a finite pore resistance ( R pore ), which became the dominant element so that V p tracked a linearly scaled V m (Fig. 3c(ii) ). Circuit simulations (Supplementary Note 1 ) predicted that, as tiles insert, steady-state V p decreases while whole-cell voltage ( V w ) increases (Fig. 3d ), consistent with experimental recordings (Fig. 3e ). These simulations further indicated that R pore can be reliably estimated up to several GΩ (Supplementary Fig. 13 ), within the range observed when tiles insert (Fig. 1g ). Using the dual-pipette approach, we obtained pore resistances of 542 ± 231 MΩ ( n = 13 neurons), in good agreement with the coarse estimate from Fig. 1g .

### Quasi-intracellular access through DNA tiles
DNA tiles that form nanopore-like access across neuronal membranes should, in principle, support the same recording modes as nanoelectrode interfaces, including quasi-intracellular recordings analogous to nanopipettes 16 (Fig. 4a ). Numerical simulations supported this idea: as pore resistance decreased, the action potential (AP) recorded through the tile–membrane interface transitioned from a capacitively filtered extracellular waveform to a scaled intracellular waveform with increased amplitude (Supplementary Fig. 17 and Supplementary Note 2 ).

### DNA tiles enable quasi-intracellular recordings in dendrites
Quasi-intracellular strategies offer a promising route to stable, higher-throughput access to local intracellular activity 8 , 52 . To test whether DNA tiles can provide such access in dendrites, we adapted the dual-pipette configuration from Figs. 3 and 4 : one pipette established whole-cell recording at the soma, while a second, tile-loaded pipette formed a cell-attached configuration on the apical dendritic trunk of L5 pyramidal neurons ( Methods and Fig. 5a ).

### Conclusion
In summary, we explored the electrical interface between DNA tiles and live neurons. We show that DNA tiles self-insert to form membrane-spanning channels, exhibit stochastic transport reminiscent of biological ion channel gating, enable ionic transport and permit small-molecule permeability (Figs. 1 and 2 ). This access increases neuronal passive conductance without affecting membrane resistance. In our configuration, the tiles add ~2 nS of conductance, a small, non-cytotoxic leak.
Structurally, the DNA tiles resemble previous designs 37 , composed of 11 nm DNA duplexes with a 0.8 nm central cavity, allowing compact yet functional lipid membrane interfacing. Negatively charged, hydrophilic DNA strands typically show poor neuronal uptake 53 , 54 , which limits membrane-spanning applications 55 . Hydrophobic modification is a standard solution to improve membrane anchoring 23 , 29 , 56 , 57 . Cholesterol tags markedly enhance membrane adhesion 58 , accelerating tile insertion into cortical neurons, as confirmed by insertion kinetics compared with unmodified tiles (Fig. 3 ). In addition, our data suggest an alternative insertion mechanism for untagged DNA nanostructures. The link between seal resistance and insertion suggests the mechanical force on membranes to be a possible promoter of tile embedding 47 .
Such engineered probes could serve as artificial membrane components and can be fabricated with controlled dimensions for targeting specific cellular or subcellular regions 25 , 59 . Recordings across tiles show stable conductance shifts and minor resistance changes, potentially useful for conditions where high resistance drives hyperexcitability. Leak conductances critically shape neuronal signalling, including excitability, signal integration, axial filtering and network synchronization 60 – 63 , and vary with inhibition, brain state and disease 64 , 65 . Thus, engineered passive leak channels could modulate excitability drug-free 66 . In addition, DNA structures

### DNA tile insertion and electrophysiological recordings
To maintain the physiological activities of the neuron, the tile insertion, incubation and recording were all performed at 34 °C ACSF under a constant carbogen supply. Borosilicate glass pipettes (4–7 MΩ) were pulled with a pipette puller (Sutter P1000) for the whole-cell and cell-attached recording. On the day of the experiment, freshly annealed DNA tiles (1 µM in buffer solution, 10 mM Tris-HCl, 1 mM EDTA, 20 mM MgCl 2 , pH 8.0) were diluted into 50–100 nM with ACSF (125 NaCl, 2.5 KCl, 1.25 NaH 2 PO 4 , 25 NaHCO 3 , 10 glucose, 2 MgCl 2 , 2 CaCl 2 , pH 7.4, osmolarity 300–310 mOsm) and the osmolarity was balanced with sucrose (&lt;5 mM) when necessary. In some experiments, 25 µM Alexa 594 or 100 μM Alexa 488 was added to the DNA tile suspension for visualization and verification that the membrane was not ruptured. The whole-cell patch-clamp pipette was filled with internal solutions containing (in mM) 130 potassium gluconate, 7 KCl, 10 HEPES, 5 NaCl, 35 sucrose, 2 MgSO 4 , 2 sodium pyruvate, 4 Mg-ATP, 0.4 Tris GTP, 7 phosphocreatine disodium, 0.025 Alexa 594 or 0.2 Alexa 488 (pH 7.3, osmolarity 290–300 mOsm). In some experiments, 200 µM fluo4 was added to the internal solution to monitor the intracellular Ca 2+ level. L5 pyramidal neurons were randomly assigned to treatment conditions (DNA tiles and control buffer). Both groups were tested within the same brain slices and brain regions to minimize confounds induced by variability in cell health or brain slice quality.
The neurons were visualized under an infrared (IR) Dodt contrast enhancement and an IR camera (Dage-MTI, IR2000) with a 40× objective (Nikon, 0.8 NA). The whole-cell recording was first formed to measure the baseline electrical properties (baseline RMP and so on). Neurons with access resistance larger than 30 MΩ or leak current larger than 300 pA (at −75 mV voltage clamp) were discarded. A small positive pressure (~0.5 psi) was maintained at the DNA tile-carrying pipette before contacting the neurona

### Preparation of giant vesicles
GUVs were prepared using an inverted emulsion method 78 . In brief, 1,2-dimyristoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (DMPC) and biotinylated lipids were mixed at a 1,000:1 molar ratio in chloroform in a glass vial. The solvent was evaporated under vacuum for 30 min to form a dry lipid film, which was subsequently resuspended in 600 μl of mineral oil and sealed with Parafilm. The oil–lipid suspension was sonicated at 50 °C for approximately 3 h to ensure homogeneous lipid dispersion.
Aqueous droplets were generated by adding 20 μl of Tris buffer (40 mM Tris, 1 mM EDTA, 20 mM acetic acid, pH 8.0) to the oil–lipid mixture, followed by vortexing for 30 s to produce a cloudy emulsion consisting of lipid-coated water droplets. A total of 600 μl of the emulsion was gently layered onto 300 μl of the same Tris buffer to establish an oil–water interface. The sample was centrifuged at 8,000 × g for 15 min, during which monolayer-coated droplets crossed the interface and assembled into bilayered GUVs that accumulated in the aqueous phase. After centrifugation, the mineral oil supernatant was carefully removed, and the GUVs were collected from the buffer phase.

### Microfluidic channel assembly
Microfluidic channels were fabricated by sealing a thin glass coverslip to a quartz slide using medical-grade acrylic double-sided adhesive tape. The channel geometry was defined by patterned slots cut into the adhesive layer. Before assembly, the glass coverslip was treated with piranha solution (H 2 SO 4 (3%):H 2 O 2 (1%)) to render the surface hydrophilic.

### GUV imaging
GUVs were imaged using a custom-built inverted fluorescence microscope based on a Zeiss Axio Observer D1 platform. Excitation was provided by diode lasers at 561 nm and 658 nm (Laserglow Technologies). Fluorescence emission was collected through a 63× oil-immersion objective (Zeiss) and detected with an Andor iXon3 electron-multiplying charge-coupled device camera.

PMCID: PMC13293863 PMID: 42225982

### Abstract
Transmembrane ionic flow through artificial ion channels is integral to the development of biohybrid electronics, such as neural interface technologies. However, achieving accurate and stable intracellular access through these synthetic analogues has remained a challenge. Here we use DNA origami tiles (0.8 nm diameter), anchored into live neuronal membranes, both with and without cholesterol tags, to demonstrate highly stable ion transport (net ~2 nS), channel-like stochasticity and intracellular drug delivery without disrupting neuronal physiology. These results are supported by molecular dynamics simulations. Using a suite of patch-clamp techniques, including two-photon-targeted variants, we obtain repeatable intracellular and quasi-intracellular voltage measurements across DNA tiles, eliminating the need for membrane break-in even from thin dendritic structures (~1 µm), which are inaccessible with standard electrodes. This advancement establishes an ‘outside looking in’ method to probe intracellular voltage dynamics using DNA nanostructure-based transmembrane access.
Subject terms: Nanostructures, Characterization and analytical techniques, Drug delivery

### Main
Precise measurement of ionic flow across cellular membranes is fundamental when assaying bioelectricity in intact cells 1 . Traditional methods, such as whole-cell patch-clamp techniques 2 , offer invaluable insights into cellular dynamics but face major limitations, particularly when accessing smaller, more complex cellular structures or achieving stable intracellular measurements without disrupting integrity 3 . Recent bioengineering advances aim to overcome these challenges through innovations such as genetically encoded light and voltage-sensitive reporters 4 , synthetic analogues of ion channels such as carbon tiles 5 , 6 , and novel nanostructures 7 . However, achieving stable, repeatable electrical recordings with these tools remains difficult.
Artificial nanostructures—such as nanopipettes 8 , carbon nanotubes 5 , 9 , three-dimensional (3D) nanoelectrodes 10 – 12 and nanowires 13 , 14 —show promise as minimally invasive intracellular interfaces for neuronal recording 15 . Unlike traditional electrodes that often cause tissue damage, these nanoelectrodes minimally penetrate membranes, detecting subthreshold potentials, action potentials and previously inaccessible synaptic activity 16 – 19 . Yet intracellular recording still requires membrane rupture, which can disrupt physiology. Surface modifications and newer approaches to membrane access may help mitigate this issue 20 . Thus, novel nanostructures capable of self-insertion and lipid bilayer remodelling are needed to achieve seamless electrical access. Neurons rely on transmembrane ion flow for signalling 21 , and synthetically replicating this through artificial channels requires lipid bilayer membrane remodelling 22 . A promising approach uses artificial DNA tiles 23 , offering a platform for mimicking natural ion channel function. These biocompatible, ion-permissive nanostructures 24 – 26 enable transmembrane ionic transport, biosensing and membrane alteration 27 , 28 . Further modifications with hydrop

### DNA tiles enable ionic current measurements across neuronal membranes
The DNA tile assemblies feature tunable length 41 and channel size 42 , 43 . As previously reported 37 , each tile comprises 11-nm-long DNA duplexes with a 0.8 nm central cavity (Fig. 1a ). Eight single strands assemble into four duplexes; two include cholesterol molecules to facilitate membrane interfacing and two carry Cy3 or Alexa 488 for two-photon imaging. DNA sequences and chemical modifications are listed in Supplementary Table 1 , and their alignment with two-dimensional (2D) duplex maps is shown in Supplementary Fig. 1 .

### DNA tiles enable molecular delivery across neuronal membranes
Using dual-patch current-clamp recordings, we demonstrate that embedded DNA tiles enable intracellular delivery of small molecules, confirming transmembrane transport (Fig. 2 ). To validate this, we tested the transfer of a water-soluble, membrane-impermeable Alexa Fluor dye (~500 g mol −1 , negatively charged). Compared with capped tiles and control buffer, DNA tiles facilitated dye entry into neurons (Supplementary Fig. 10 ), confirming targeted molecular transport across membrane-anchored tiles.

### Characterization of pore resistance in neuronal membranes
The voltage-clamp recordings in Fig. 1 established DNA tile insertion into neuronal membranes via conductance changes but did not allow precise estimation of pore resistance owing to circuit constraints (Supplementary Note 1 ). To refine these measurements, we used a dual-pipette configuration ( Methods and Fig. 3a ). Two-photon imaging confirmed that tiles remained confined to the membrane patch in the cell-attached pipette, with no fluorescence wash-in, indicating that membrane integrity was preserved (Fig. 3b ). We analytically solved the equivalent circuit of the dual recording before and after tile insertion (Fig. 3c and Supplementary Fig. 13a ). Before insertion, the pipette voltage ( V p ) was dominated by the membrane capacitance (Fig. 3c(i) ), acting as a high-pass filter of the membrane voltage ( V m ) 46 . Upon tile insertion, ion permeability introduced a finite pore resistance ( R pore ), which became the dominant element so that V p tracked a linearly scaled V m (Fig. 3c(ii) ). Circuit simulations (Supplementary Note 1 ) predicted that, as tiles insert, steady-state V p decreases while whole-cell voltage ( V w ) increases (Fig. 3d ), consistent with experimental recordings (Fig. 3e ). These simulations further indicated that R pore can be reliably estimated up to several GΩ (Supplementary Fig. 13 ), within the range observed when tiles insert (Fig. 1g ). Using the dual-pipette approach, we obtained pore resistances of 542 ± 231 MΩ ( n = 13 neurons), in good agreement with the coarse estimate from Fig. 1g .

### Fig. 3. Estimation of tile resistance.
a , Schematic of the dual-pipette experimental set-up in which one pipette is loaded with DNA tiles and sealed to the cell membrane (black), while a second pipette is loaded with intracellular solution performing a conventional whole-cell patch-clamp recording (red). b , A two-photon image of the dual-patch set-up described in a . Scale bar, 20 µm. c , Equivalent circuit diagram describing the interface between the cell-attached pipette before (i) and after (ii) tile insertion. Upon insertion, the recorded pipette voltage ( V p ) will change from an extracellular capacitive-filtered waveform to a linearly scaled one (quasi-intracellular recording). d , Numerical simulation of steady-state cell-attached (blue) and whole-cell (red) voltages as a function of pore resistance. R seal = 75 MΩ, C m = 60 pF, R m = 55.6 MΩ. e , Evolution of voltage recordings from the whole-cell and cell-attached electrodes during the tile insertion. f , (i) No change in neuron input resistance (left) and intracellular Ca 2+ level (right) before (black) and after (red) tile insertion (two-sided paired-sample t -test, R in , n = 11 neurons; Ca 2+ level, n = 9 neurons). (ii) Similar pore resistance revealed by DNA tiles with (red) and without (black) functional cholesterol tags upon neuronal membrane insertion (two-sided Mann–Whitney–Wilcoxon test, n = 9 neurons with cholesterol, 7 neurons without cholesterol). g , Schematic outlining the possible mechanism facilitating tile insertion in which adhesion force between the membrane-glass interface and lipids helps drive DNA tile insertion, including without cholesterol tags. h , The tile insertion time decreases with increased seal resistance ( n = 23 neurons, F (1) = 5.95, one-way ANOVA). i , Cholesterol tags speed up tile insertion (Mann–Whitney–Wilcoxon test, n = 9 neurons with cholesterol, 5 neurons without cholesterol). ### Quasi-intracellular access through DNA tiles
DNA tiles that form nanopore-like access across neuronal membranes should, in principle, support the same recording modes as nanoelectrode interfaces, including quasi-intracellular recordings analogous to nanopipettes 16 (Fig. 4a ). Numerical simulations supported this idea: as pore resistance decreased, the action potential (AP) recorded through the tile–membrane interface transitioned from a capacitively filtered extracellular waveform to a scaled intracellular waveform with increased amplitude (Supplementary Fig. 17 and Supplementary Note 2 ).

Insets show the AP waveform recorded from the cell-attached pipette at two time points. Scale bar, left, 5 ms, 0.1 mV; right, 5 ms, 5 mV. c , AP amplitude measured from the cell-attached pipette before ( t = 0; black) and after ( t = 10–20 min; red) tile insertion under loose-seal (left, R seal &lt; 0.3 GΩ) and tight-seal (right, R seal &gt; 1 GΩ) configuration (loose seal, n = 6 neurons; tight seal, n = 5 neurons, paired-sample t -test). The centre and the bounds of the box plots represent 50%, 25% and 75% percentiles, and the whiskers represent 1.5 interquartile range below/above the first or the third quartile. d , DNA tiles facilitate stable repeatable cell-attached quasi-intracellular measures. Top: the dual-pipette configuration. Middle: whole-cell intracellular recording (red). Bottom: cell-attached recording (black). (i) Initial loose-seal configuration with the cell-attached pipette just brought in contact with the whole-cell patched neuron, evident by the capacitive AP waveforms. (ii) Insertion of tiles reveals ohmic quasi-intracellular recordings. (iii) The cell-attached pipette is retracted, signalling a loss in quasi-intracellular recordings. (iv) After ~5–10 min, the cell-attached pipette is brought back in contact with the same patch of cell membrane populated with tiles. Note the near-immediate reflection of spikes. (v) Within a minute of reattaching the quasi-intracellular waveforms emerge.

### DNA tiles enable quasi-intracellular recordings in dendrites
Quasi-intracellular strategies offer a promising route to stable, higher-throughput access to local intracellular activity 8 , 52 . To test whether DNA tiles can provide such access in dendrites, we adapted the dual-pipette configuration from Figs. 3 and 4 : one pipette established whole-cell recording at the soma, while a second, tile-loaded pipette formed a cell-attached configuration on the apical dendritic trunk of L5 pyramidal neurons ( Methods and Fig. 5a ).

### Conclusion
In summary, we explored the electrical interface between DNA tiles and live neurons. We show that DNA tiles self-insert to form membrane-spanning channels, exhibit stochastic transport reminiscent of biological ion channel gating, enable ionic transport and permit small-molecule permeability (Figs. 1 and 2 ). This access increases neuronal passive conductance without affecting membrane resistance. In our configuration, the tiles add ~2 nS of conductance, a small, non-cytotoxic leak.
Structurally, the DNA tiles resemble previous designs 37 , composed of 11 nm DNA duplexes with a 0.8 nm central cavity, allowing compact yet functional lipid membrane interfacing. Negatively charged, hydrophilic DNA strands typically show poor neuronal uptake 53 , 54 , which limits membrane-spanning applications 55 . Hydrophobic modification is a standard solution to improve membrane anchoring 23 , 29 , 56 , 57 . Cholesterol tags markedly enhance membrane adhesion 58 , accelerating tile insertion into cortical neurons, as confirmed by insertion kinetics compared with unmodified tiles (Fig. 3 ). In addition, our data suggest an alternative insertion mechanism for untagged DNA nanostructures. The link between seal resistance and insertion suggests the mechanical force on membranes to be a possible promoter of tile embedding 47 .
Such engineered probes could serve as artificial membrane components and can be fabricated with controlled dimensions for targeting specific cellular or subcellular regions 25 , 59 . Recordings across tiles show stable conductance shifts and minor resistance changes, potentially useful for conditions where high resistance drives hyperexcitability. Leak conductances critically shape neuronal signalling, including excitability, signal integration, axial filtering and network synchronization 60 – 63 , and vary with inhibition, brain state and disease 64 , 65 . Thus, engineered passive leak channels could modulate excitability drug-free 66 . In addition, DNA structures

### DNA tile insertion and electrophysiological recordings
To maintain the physiological activities of the neuron, the tile insertion, incubation and recording were all performed at 34 °C ACSF under a constant carbogen supply. Borosilicate glass pipettes (4–7 MΩ) were pulled with a pipette puller (Sutter P1000) for the whole-cell and cell-attached recording. On the day of the experiment, freshly annealed DNA tiles (1 µM in buffer solution, 10 mM Tris-HCl, 1 mM EDTA, 20 mM MgCl 2 , pH 8.0) were diluted into 50–100 nM with ACSF (125 NaCl, 2.5 KCl, 1.25 NaH 2 PO 4 , 25 NaHCO 3 , 10 glucose, 2 MgCl 2 , 2 CaCl 2 , pH 7.4, osmolarity 300–310 mOsm) and the osmolarity was balanced with sucrose (&lt;5 mM) when necessary. In some experiments, 25 µM Alexa 594 or 100 μM Alexa 488 was added to the DNA tile suspension for visualization and verification that the membrane was not ruptured. The whole-cell patch-clamp pipette was filled with internal solutions containing (in mM) 130 potassium gluconate, 7 KCl, 10 HEPES, 5 NaCl, 35 sucrose, 2 MgSO 4 , 2 sodium pyruvate, 4 Mg-ATP, 0.4 Tris GTP, 7 phosphocreatine disodium, 0.025 Alexa 594 or 0.2 Alexa 488 (pH 7.3, osmolarity 290–300 mOsm). In some experiments, 200 µM fluo4 was added to the internal solution to monitor the intracellular Ca 2+ level. L5 pyramidal neurons were randomly assigned to treatment conditions (DNA tiles and control buffer). Both groups were tested within the same brain slices and brain regions to minimize confounds induced by variability in cell health or brain slice quality.
The neurons were visualized under an infrared (IR) Dodt contrast enhancement and an IR camera (Dage-MTI, IR2000) with a 40× objective (Nikon, 0.8 NA). The whole-cell recording was first formed to measure the baseline electrical properties (baseline RMP and so on). Neurons with access resistance larger than 30 MΩ or leak current larger than 300 pA (at −75 mV voltage clamp) were discarded. A small positive pressure (~0.5 psi) was maintained at the DNA tile-carrying pipette before contacting the neurona

### Preparation of giant vesicles
GUVs were prepared using an inverted emulsion method 78 . In brief, 1,2-dimyristoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (DMPC) and biotinylated lipids were mixed at a 1,000:1 molar ratio in chloroform in a glass vial. The solvent was evaporated under vacuum for 30 min to form a dry lipid film, which was subsequently resuspended in 600 μl of mineral oil and sealed with Parafilm. The oil–lipid suspension was sonicated at 50 °C for approximately 3 h to ensure homogeneous lipid dispersion.
Aqueous droplets were generated by adding 20 μl of Tris buffer (40 mM Tris, 1 mM EDTA, 20 mM acetic acid, pH 8.0) to the oil–lipid mixture, followed by vortexing for 30 s to produce a cloudy emulsion consisting of lipid-coated water droplets. A total of 600 μl of the emulsion was gently layered onto 300 μl of the same Tris buffer to establish an oil–water interface. The sample was centrifuged at 8,000 × g for 15 min, during which monolayer-coated droplets crossed the interface and assembled into bilayered GUVs that accumulated in the aqueous phase. After centrifugation, the mineral oil supernatant was carefully removed, and the GUVs were collected from the buffer phase.

### Microfluidic channel assembly
Microfluidic channels were fabricated by sealing a thin glass coverslip to a quartz slide using medical-grade acrylic double-sided adhesive tape. The channel geometry was defined by patterned slots cut into the adhesive layer. Before assembly, the glass coverslip was treated with piranha solution (H 2 SO 4 (3%):H 2 O 2 (1%)) to render the surface hydrophilic.

### GUV imaging
GUVs were imaged using a custom-built inverted fluorescence microscope based on a Zeiss Axio Observer D1 platform. Excitation was provided by diode lasers at 561 nm and 658 nm (Laserglow Technologies). Fluorescence emission was collected through a 63× oil-immersion objective (Zeiss) and detected with an Andor iXon3 electron-multiplying charge-coupled device camera.

### Abstract
Transmembrane ionic flow through artificial ion channels is integral to the development of biohybrid electronics, such as neural interface technologies. However, achieving accurate and stable intracellular access through these synthetic analogues has remained a challenge. Here we use DNA origami tiles (0.8 nm diameter), anchored into live neuronal membranes, both with and without cholesterol tags, to demonstrate highly stable ion transport (net ~2 nS), channel-like stochasticity and intracellular drug delivery without disrupting neuronal physiology. These results are supported by molecular dynamics simulations. Using a suite of patch-clamp techniques, including two-photon-targeted variants, we obtain repeatable intracellular and quasi-intracellular voltage measurements across DNA tiles, eliminating the need for membrane break-in even from thin dendritic structures (~1 µm), which are inaccessible with standard electrodes. This advancement establishes an ‘outside looking in’ method to probe intracellular voltage dynamics using DNA nanostructure-based transmembrane access.
Subject terms: Nanostructures, Characterization and analytical techniques, Drug delivery

### Main
Precise measurement of ionic flow across cellular membranes is fundamental when assaying bioelectricity in intact cells 1 . Traditional methods, such as whole-cell patch-clamp techniques 2 , offer invaluable insights into cellular dynamics but face major limitations, particularly when accessing smaller, more complex cellular structures or achieving stable intracellular measurements without disrupting integrity 3 . Recent bioengineering advances aim to overcome these challenges through innovations such as genetically encoded light and voltage-sensitive reporters 4 , synthetic analogues of ion channels such as carbon tiles 5 , 6 , and novel nanostructures 7 . However, achieving stable, repeatable electrical recordings with these tools remains difficult.
Artificial nanostructures—such as nanopipettes 8 , carbon nanotubes 5 , 9 , three-dimensional (3D) nanoelectrodes 10 – 12 and nanowires 13 , 14 —show promise as minimally invasive intracellular interfaces for neuronal recording 15 . Unlike traditional electrodes that often cause tissue damage, these nanoelectrodes minimally penetrate membranes, detecting subthreshold potentials, action potentials and previously inaccessible synaptic activity 16 – 19 . Yet intracellular recording still requires membrane rupture, which can disrupt physiology. Surface modifications and newer approaches to membrane access may help mitigate this issue 20 . Thus, novel nanostructures capable of self-insertion and lipid bilayer remodelling are needed to achieve seamless electrical access. Neurons rely on transmembrane ion flow for signalling 21 , and synthetically replicating this through artificial channels requires lipid bilayer membrane remodelling 22 . A promising approach uses artificial DNA tiles 23 , offering a platform for mimicking natural ion channel function. These biocompatible, ion-permissive nanostructures 24 – 26 enable transmembrane ionic transport, biosensing and membrane alteration 27 , 28 . Further modifications with hydrop

### DNA tiles enable ionic current measurements across neuronal membranes
The DNA tile assemblies feature tunable length 41 and channel size 42 , 43 . As previously reported 37 , each tile comprises 11-nm-long DNA duplexes with a 0.8 nm central cavity (Fig. 1a ). Eight single strands assemble into four duplexes; two include cholesterol molecules to facilitate membrane interfacing and two carry Cy3 or Alexa 488 for two-photon imaging. DNA sequences and chemical modifications are listed in Supplementary Table 1 , and their alignment with two-dimensional (2D) duplex maps is shown in Supplementary Fig. 1 .

### DNA tiles enable molecular delivery across neuronal membranes
Using dual-patch current-clamp recordings, we demonstrate that embedded DNA tiles enable intracellular delivery of small molecules, confirming transmembrane transport (Fig. 2 ). To validate this, we tested the transfer of a water-soluble, membrane-impermeable Alexa Fluor dye (~500 g mol −1 , negatively charged). Compared with capped tiles and control buffer, DNA tiles facilitated dye entry into neurons (Supplementary Fig. 10 ), confirming targeted molecular transport across membrane-anchored tiles.

### Characterization of pore resistance in neuronal membranes
The voltage-clamp recordings in Fig. 1 established DNA tile insertion into neuronal membranes via conductance changes but did not allow precise estimation of pore resistance owing to circuit constraints (Supplementary Note 1 ). To refine these measurements, we used a dual-pipette configuration ( Methods and Fig. 3a ). Two-photon imaging confirmed that tiles remained confined to the membrane patch in the cell-attached pipette, with no fluorescence wash-in, indicating that membrane integrity was preserved (Fig. 3b ). We analytically solved the equivalent circuit of the dual recording before and after tile insertion (Fig. 3c and Supplementary Fig. 13a ). Before insertion, the pipette voltage ( V p ) was dominated by the membrane capacitance (Fig. 3c(i) ), acting as a high-pass filter of the membrane voltage ( V m ) 46 . Upon tile insertion, ion permeability introduced a finite pore resistance ( R pore ), which became the dominant element so that V p tracked a linearly scaled V m (Fig. 3c(ii) ). Circuit simulations (Supplementary Note 1 ) predicted that, as tiles insert, steady-state V p decreases while whole-cell voltage ( V w ) increases (Fig. 3d ), consistent with experimental recordings (Fig. 3e ). These simulations further indicated that R pore can be reliably estimated up to several GΩ (Supplementary Fig. 13 ), within the range observed when tiles insert (Fig. 1g ). Using the dual-pipette approach, we obtained pore resistances of 542 ± 231 MΩ ( n = 13 neurons), in good agreement with the coarse estimate from Fig. 1g .

### Fig. 3. Estimation of tile resistance.
a , Schematic of the dual-pipette experimental set-up in which one pipette is loaded with DNA tiles and sealed to the cell membrane (black), while a second pipette is loaded with intracellular solution performing a conventional whole-cell patch-clamp recording (red). b , A two-photon image of the dual-patch set-up described in a . Scale bar, 20 µm. c , Equivalent circuit diagram describing the interface between the cell-attached pipette before (i) and after (ii) tile insertion. Upon insertion, the recorded pipette voltage ( V p ) will change from an extracellular capacitive-filtered waveform to a linearly scaled one (quasi-intracellular recording). d , Numerical simulation of steady-state cell-attached (blue) and whole-cell (red) voltages as a function of pore resistance. R seal = 75 MΩ, C m = 60 pF, R m = 55.6 MΩ. e , Evolution of voltage recordings from the whole-cell and cell-attached electrodes during the tile insertion. f , (i) No change in neuron input resistance (left) and intracellular Ca 2+ level (right) before (black) and after (red) tile insertion (two-sided paired-sample t -test, R in , n = 11 neurons; Ca 2+ level, n = 9 neurons). (ii) Similar pore resistance revealed by DNA tiles with (red) and without (black) functional cholesterol tags upon neuronal membrane insertion (two-sided Mann–Whitney–Wilcoxon test, n = 9 neurons with cholesterol, 7 neurons without cholesterol). g , Schematic outlining the possible mechanism facilitating tile insertion in which adhesion force between the membrane-glass interface and lipids helps drive DNA tile insertion, including without cholesterol tags. h , The tile insertion time decreases with increased seal resistance ( n = 23 neurons, F (1) = 5.95, one-way ANOVA). i , Cholesterol tags speed up tile insertion (Mann–Whitney–Wilcoxon test, n = 9 neurons with cholesterol, 5 neurons without cholesterol). The centre and the bounds of the box plots in f and i represent 50%, 25% and 75% percentiles, and the whiskers represent 1.

### Quasi-intracellular access through DNA tiles
DNA tiles that form nanopore-like access across neuronal membranes should, in principle, support the same recording modes as nanoelectrode interfaces, including quasi-intracellular recordings analogous to nanopipettes 16 (Fig. 4a ). Numerical simulations supported this idea: as pore resistance decreased, the action potential (AP) recorded through the tile–membrane interface transitioned from a capacitively filtered extracellular waveform to a scaled intracellular waveform with increased amplitude (Supplementary Fig. 17 and Supplementary Note 2 ).

### Fig. 4. Quasi-intracellular recording across DNA tiles.
a , Schematic of the dual-patch set-up. b , APs recorded from the whole-cell (red) and cell-attached (black) electrode during tile insertion. Left: capacitively coupled spike waveforms observed before the DNA tiles self-inserted. Right: a DC shift and a one-to-one correspondence to the intracellular spikes after about 10 min when DNA tiles self-inserted into the membrane. Insets show the AP waveform recorded from the cell-attached pipette at two time points. Scale bar, left, 5 ms, 0.1 mV; right, 5 ms, 5 mV. c , AP amplitude measured from the cell-attached pipette before ( t = 0; black) and after ( t = 10–20 min; red) tile insertion under loose-seal (left, R seal &lt; 0.3 GΩ) and tight-seal (right, R seal &gt; 1 GΩ) configuration (loose seal, n = 6 neurons; tight seal, n = 5 neurons, paired-sample t -test). The centre and the bounds of the box plots represent 50%, 25% and 75% percentiles, and the whiskers represent 1.5 interquartile range below/above the first or the third quartile. d , DNA tiles facilitate stable repeatable cell-attached quasi-intracellular measures. Top: the dual-pipette configuration. Middle: whole-cell intracellular recording (red). Bottom: cell-attached recording (black). (i) Initial loose-seal configuration with the cell-attached pipette just brought in contact with the whole-cell patched neuron, evident by the capacitive AP waveforms. (ii) Insertion of tiles reveals ohmic quasi-intracellular recordings. (iii) The cell-attached pipette is retracted, signalling a loss in quasi-intracellular recordings. (iv) After ~5–10 min, the cell-attached pipette is brought back in contact with the same patch of cell membrane populated with tiles. Note the near-immediate reflection of spikes. (v) Within a minute of reattaching the quasi-intracellular waveforms emerge.
Source data Using the dual-pipette configuration, we observed the same behaviour experimentally (Fig. 4a,b ). After tile insertion, the cell-attached electrode reported subthreshold depolarizati

### DNA tiles enable quasi-intracellular recordings in dendrites
Quasi-intracellular strategies offer a promising route to stable, higher-throughput access to local intracellular activity 8 , 52 . To test whether DNA tiles can provide such access in dendrites, we adapted the dual-pipette configuration from Figs. 3 and 4 : one pipette established whole-cell recording at the soma, while a second, tile-loaded pipette formed a cell-attached configuration on the apical dendritic trunk of L5 pyramidal neurons ( Methods and Fig. 5a ).

### Conclusion
In summary, we explored the electrical interface between DNA tiles and live neurons. We show that DNA tiles self-insert to form membrane-spanning channels, exhibit stochastic transport reminiscent of biological ion channel gating, enable ionic transport and permit small-molecule permeability (Figs. 1 and 2 ). This access increases neuronal passive conductance without affecting membrane resistance. In our configuration, the tiles add ~2 nS of conductance, a small, non-cytotoxic leak.
Structurally, the DNA tiles resemble previous designs 37 , composed of 11 nm DNA duplexes with a 0.8 nm central cavity, allowing compact yet functional lipid membrane interfacing. Negatively charged, hydrophilic DNA strands typically show poor neuronal uptake 53 , 54 , which limits membrane-spanning applications 55 . Hydrophobic modification is a standard solution to improve membrane anchoring 23 , 29 , 56 , 57 . Cholesterol tags markedly enhance membrane adhesion 58 , accelerating tile insertion into cortical neurons, as confirmed by insertion kinetics compared with unmodified tiles (Fig. 3 ). In addition, our data suggest an alternative insertion mechanism for untagged DNA nanostructures. The link between seal resistance and insertion suggests the mechanical force on membranes to be a possible promoter of tile embedding 47 .
Such engineered probes could serve as artificial membrane components and can be fabricated with controlled dimensions for targeting specific cellular or subcellular regions 25 , 59 . Recordings across tiles show stable conductance shifts and minor resistance changes, potentially useful for conditions where high resistance drives hyperexcitability. Leak conductances critically shape neuronal signalling, including excitability, signal integration, axial filtering and network synchronization 60 – 63 , and vary with inhibition, brain state and disease 64 , 65 . Thus, engineered passive leak channels could modulate excitability drug-free 66 . In addition, DNA structures

### DNA tile insertion and electrophysiological recordings
To maintain the physiological activities of the neuron, the tile insertion, incubation and recording were all performed at 34 °C ACSF under a constant carbogen supply. Borosilicate glass pipettes (4–7 MΩ) were pulled with a pipette puller (Sutter P1000) for the whole-cell and cell-attached recording. On the day of the experiment, freshly annealed DNA tiles (1 µM in buffer solution, 10 mM Tris-HCl, 1 mM EDTA, 20 mM MgCl 2 , pH 8.0) were diluted into 50–100 nM with ACSF (125 NaCl, 2.5 KCl, 1.25 NaH 2 PO 4 , 25 NaHCO 3 , 10 glucose, 2 MgCl 2 , 2 CaCl 2 , pH 7.4, osmolarity 300–310 mOsm) and the osmolarity was balanced with sucrose (&lt;5 mM) when necessary. In some experiments, 25 µM Alexa 594 or 100 μM Alexa 488 was added to the DNA tile suspension for visualization and verification that the membrane was not ruptured. The whole-cell patch-clamp pipette was filled with internal solutions containing (in mM) 130 potassium gluconate, 7 KCl, 10 HEPES, 5 NaCl, 35 sucrose, 2 MgSO 4 , 2 sodium pyruvate, 4 Mg-ATP, 0.4 Tris GTP, 7 phosphocreatine disodium, 0.025 Alexa 594 or 0.2 Alexa 488 (pH 7.3, osmolarity 290–300 mOsm). In some experiments, 200 µM fluo4 was added to the internal solution to monitor the intracellular Ca 2+ level. L5 pyramidal neurons were randomly assigned to treatment conditions (DNA tiles and control buffer). Both groups were tested within the same brain slices and brain regions to minimize confounds induced by variability in cell health or brain slice quality.
The neurons were visualized under an infrared (IR) Dodt contrast enhancement and an IR camera (Dage-MTI, IR2000) with a 40× objective (Nikon, 0.8 NA). The whole-cell recording was first formed to measure the baseline electrical properties (baseline RMP and so on). Neurons with access resistance larger than 30 MΩ or leak current larger than 300 pA (at −75 mV voltage clamp) were discarded. A small positive pressure (~0.5 psi) was maintained at the DNA tile-carrying pipette before contacting the neurona

### Preparation of giant vesicles
GUVs were prepared using an inverted emulsion method 78 . In brief, 1,2-dimyristoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (DMPC) and biotinylated lipids were mixed at a 1,000:1 molar ratio in chloroform in a glass vial. The solvent was evaporated under vacuum for 30 min to form a dry lipid film, which was subsequently resuspended in 600 μl of mineral oil and sealed with Parafilm. The oil–lipid suspension was sonicated at 50 °C for approximately 3 h to ensure homogeneous lipid dispersion.
Aqueous droplets were generated by adding 20 μl of Tris buffer (40 mM Tris, 1 mM EDTA, 20 mM acetic acid, pH 8.0) to the oil–lipid mixture, followed by vortexing for 30 s to produce a cloudy emulsion consisting of lipid-coated water droplets. A total of 600 μl of the emulsion was gently layered onto 300 μl of the same Tris buffer to establish an oil–water interface. The sample was centrifuged at 8,000 × g for 15 min, during which monolayer-coated droplets crossed the interface and assembled into bilayered GUVs that accumulated in the aqueous phase. After centrifugation, the mineral oil supernatant was carefully removed, and the GUVs were collected from the buffer phase.

### Microfluidic channel assembly
Microfluidic channels were fabricated by sealing a thin glass coverslip to a quartz slide using medical-grade acrylic double-sided adhesive tape. The channel geometry was defined by patterned slots cut into the adhesive layer. Before assembly, the glass coverslip was treated with piranha solution (H 2 SO 4 (3%):H 2 O 2 (1%)) to render the surface hydrophilic.

### GUV imaging
GUVs were imaged using a custom-built inverted fluorescence microscope based on a Zeiss Axio Observer D1 platform. Excitation was provided by diode lasers at 561 nm and 658 nm (Laserglow Technologies). Fluorescence emission was collected through a 63× oil-immersion objective (Zeiss) and detected with an Andor iXon3 electron-multiplying charge-coupled device camera.

### Abstract
Transmembrane ionic flow through artificial ion channels is integral to the development of biohybrid electronics, such as neural interface technologies. However, achieving accurate and stable intracellular access through these synthetic analogues has remained a challenge. Here we use DNA origami tiles (0.8 nm diameter), anchored into live neuronal membranes, both with and without cholesterol tags, to demonstrate highly stable ion transport (net ~2 nS), channel-like stochasticity and intracellular drug delivery without disrupting neuronal physiology. These results are supported by molecular dynamics simulations. Using a suite of patch-clamp techniques, including two-photon-targeted variants, we obtain repeatable intracellular and quasi-intracellular voltage measurements across DNA tiles, eliminating the need for membrane break-in even from thin dendritic structures (~1 µm), which are inaccessible with standard electrodes. This advancement establishes an ‘outside looking in’ method to probe intracellular voltage dynamics using DNA nanostructure-based transmembrane access.
Subject terms: Nanostructures, Characterization and analytical techniques, Drug delivery

### Main
Precise measurement of ionic flow across cellular membranes is fundamental when assaying bioelectricity in intact cells 1 . Traditional methods, such as whole-cell patch-clamp techniques 2 , offer invaluable insights into cellular dynamics but face major limitations, particularly when accessing smaller, more complex cellular structures or achieving stable intracellular measurements without disrupting integrity 3 . Recent bioengineering advances aim to overcome these challenges through innovations such as genetically encoded light and voltage-sensitive reporters 4 , synthetic analogues of ion channels such as carbon tiles 5 , 6 , and novel nanostructures 7 . However, achieving stable, repeatable electrical recordings with these tools remains difficult.
Artificial nanostructures—such as nanopipettes 8 , carbon nanotubes 5 , 9 , three-dimensional (3D) nanoelectrodes 10 – 12 and nanowires 13 , 14 —show promise as minimally invasive intracellular interfaces for neuronal recording 15 . Unlike traditional electrodes that often cause tissue damage, these nanoelectrodes minimally penetrate membranes, detecting subthreshold potentials, action potentials and previously inaccessible synaptic activity 16 – 19 . Yet intracellular recording still requires membrane rupture, which can disrupt physiology. Surface modifications and newer approaches to membrane access may help mitigate this issue 20 . Thus, novel nanostructures capable of self-insertion and lipid bilayer remodelling are needed to achieve seamless electrical access. Neurons rely on transmembrane ion flow for signalling 21 , and synthetically replicating this through artificial channels requires lipid bilayer membrane remodelling 22 . A promising approach uses artificial DNA tiles 23 , offering a platform for mimicking natural ion channel function. These biocompatible, ion-permissive nanostructures 24 – 26 enable transmembrane ionic transport, biosensing and membrane alteration 27 , 28 . Further modifications with hydrop

### DNA tiles enable ionic current measurements across neuronal membranes
The DNA tile assemblies feature tunable length 41 and channel size 42 , 43 . As previously reported 37 , each tile comprises 11-nm-long DNA duplexes with a 0.8 nm central cavity (Fig. 1a ). Eight single strands assemble into four duplexes; two include cholesterol molecules to facilitate membrane interfacing and two carry Cy3 or Alexa 488 for two-photon imaging. DNA sequences and chemical modifications are listed in Supplementary Table 1 , and their alignment with two-dimensional (2D) duplex maps is shown in Supplementary Fig. 1 .

### Fig. 1. Design and characterization of neuronal membrane-spanning DNA tiles.
a , (i) Schematic 3D design of a DNA tile comprising four connected duplexes, two cholesterol tags and two Cy3 (or Alexa 488) tags. (ii) Schematic showing how DNA tiles insert onto neuronal membranes and enable intracellular electrical access. Inset: circuit schematic of the lipid membrane with embedded DNA tiles. b , Polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (6%). Lane 1: gene ruler low-range DNA ladder. Lane 2: single DNA strand (28 bp). Lane 3: DNA tile structure without two DNA strands. Lane 4: complete DNA tile structure without cholesterol tags. Lane 5: complete DNA tile structure with cholesterol tags. c , Atomic force microscope image of DNA tiles. d , (i) Schematic of the experimental set-up in which DNA tiles are directed into the neuronal membrane via a patch pipette that gently seals onto the membrane. ### DNA tiles enable molecular delivery across neuronal membranes
Using dual-patch current-clamp recordings, we demonstrate that embedded DNA tiles enable intracellular delivery of small molecules, confirming transmembrane transport (Fig. 2 ). To validate this, we tested the transfer of a water-soluble, membrane-impermeable Alexa Fluor dye (~500 g mol −1 , negatively charged). Compared with capped tiles and control buffer, DNA tiles facilitated dye entry into neurons (Supplementary Fig. 10 ), confirming targeted molecular transport across membrane-anchored tiles.

### Characterization of pore resistance in neuronal membranes
The voltage-clamp recordings in Fig. 1 established DNA tile insertion into neuronal membranes via conductance changes but did not allow precise estimation of pore resistance owing to circuit constraints (Supplementary Note 1 ). To refine these measurements, we used a dual-pipette configuration ( Methods and Fig. 3a ). Two-photon imaging confirmed that tiles remained confined to the membrane patch in the cell-attached pipette, with no fluorescence wash-in, indicating that membrane integrity was preserved (Fig. 3b ). We analytically solved the equivalent circuit of the dual recording before and after tile insertion (Fig. 3c and Supplementary Fig. 13a ). Before insertion, the pipette voltage ( V p ) was dominated by the membrane capacitance (Fig. 3c(i) ), acting as a high-pass filter of the membrane voltage ( V m ) 46 . Upon tile insertion, ion permeability introduced a finite pore resistance ( R pore ), which became the dominant element so that V p tracked a linearly scaled V m (Fig. 3c(ii) ). Circuit simulations (Supplementary Note 1 ) predicted that, as tiles insert, steady-state V p decreases while whole-cell voltage ( V w ) increases (Fig. 3d ), consistent with experimental recordings (Fig. 3e ). These simulations further indicated that R pore can be reliably estimated up to several GΩ (Supplementary Fig. 13 ), within the range observed when tiles insert (Fig. 1g ). Using the dual-pipette approach, we obtained pore resistances of 542 ± 231 MΩ ( n = 13 neurons), in good agreement with the coarse estimate from Fig. 1g .

### Quasi-intracellular access through DNA tiles
DNA tiles that form nanopore-like access across neuronal membranes should, in principle, support the same recording modes as nanoelectrode interfaces, including quasi-intracellular recordings analogous to nanopipettes 16 (Fig. 4a ). Numerical simulations supported this idea: as pore resistance decreased, the action potential (AP) recorded through the tile–membrane interface transitioned from a capacitively filtered extracellular waveform to a scaled intracellular waveform with increased amplitude (Supplementary Fig. 17 and Supplementary Note 2 ).

### DNA tiles enable quasi-intracellular recordings in dendrites
Quasi-intracellular strategies offer a promising route to stable, higher-throughput access to local intracellular activity 8 , 52 . To test whether DNA tiles can provide such access in dendrites, we adapted the dual-pipette configuration from Figs. 3 and 4 : one pipette established whole-cell recording at the soma, while a second, tile-loaded pipette formed a cell-attached configuration on the apical dendritic trunk of L5 pyramidal neurons ( Methods and Fig. 5a ).

### Conclusion
In summary, we explored the electrical interface between DNA tiles and live neurons. We show that DNA tiles self-insert to form membrane-spanning channels, exhibit stochastic transport reminiscent of biological ion channel gating, enable ionic transport and permit small-molecule permeability (Figs. 1 and 2 ). This access increases neuronal passive conductance without affecting membrane resistance. In our configuration, the tiles add ~2 nS of conductance, a small, non-cytotoxic leak.
Structurally, the DNA tiles resemble previous designs 37 , composed of 11 nm DNA duplexes with a 0.8 nm central cavity, allowing compact yet functional lipid membrane interfacing. Negatively charged, hydrophilic DNA strands typically show poor neuronal uptake 53 , 54 , which limits membrane-spanning applications 55 . Hydrophobic modification is a standard solution to improve membrane anchoring 23 , 29 , 56 , 57 . Cholesterol tags markedly enhance membrane adhesion 58 , accelerating tile insertion into cortical neurons, as confirmed by insertion kinetics compared with unmodified tiles (Fig. 3 ). In addition, our data suggest an alternative insertion mechanism for untagged DNA nanostructures. The link between seal resistance and insertion suggests the mechanical force on membranes to be a possible promoter of tile embedding 47 .
Such engineered probes could serve as artificial membrane components and can be fabricated with controlled dimensions for targeting specific cellular or subcellular regions 25 , 59 . Recordings across tiles show stable conductance shifts and minor resistance changes, potentially useful for conditions where high resistance drives hyperexcitability. Leak conductances critically shape neuronal signalling, including excitability, signal integration, axial filtering and network synchronization 60 – 63 , and vary with inhibition, brain state and disease 64 , 65 . Thus, engineered passive leak channels could modulate excitability drug-free 66 . In addition, DNA structures

### DNA tile insertion and electrophysiological recordings
To maintain the physiological activities of the neuron, the tile insertion, incubation and recording were all performed at 34 °C ACSF under a constant carbogen supply. Borosilicate glass pipettes (4–7 MΩ) were pulled with a pipette puller (Sutter P1000) for the whole-cell and cell-attached recording. On the day of the experiment, freshly annealed DNA tiles (1 µM in buffer solution, 10 mM Tris-HCl, 1 mM EDTA, 20 mM MgCl 2 , pH 8.0) were diluted into 50–100 nM with ACSF (125 NaCl, 2.5 KCl, 1.25 NaH 2 PO 4 , 25 NaHCO 3 , 10 glucose, 2 MgCl 2 , 2 CaCl 2 , pH 7.4, osmolarity 300–310 mOsm) and the osmolarity was balanced with sucrose (&lt;5 mM) when necessary. In some experiments, 25 µM Alexa 594 or 100 μM Alexa 488 was added to the DNA tile suspension for visualization and verification that the membrane was not ruptured. The whole-cell patch-clamp pipette was filled with internal solutions containing (in mM) 130 potassium gluconate, 7 KCl, 10 HEPES, 5 NaCl, 35 sucrose, 2 MgSO 4 , 2 sodium pyruvate, 4 Mg-ATP, 0.4 Tris GTP, 7 phosphocreatine disodium, 0.025 Alexa 594 or 0.2 Alexa 488 (pH 7.3, osmolarity 290–300 mOsm). In some experiments, 200 µM fluo4 was added to the internal solution to monitor the intracellular Ca 2+ level. L5 pyramidal neurons were randomly assigned to treatment conditions (DNA tiles and control buffer). Both groups were tested within the same brain slices and brain regions to minimize confounds induced by variability in cell health or brain slice quality.
The neurons were visualized under an infrared (IR) Dodt contrast enhancement and an IR camera (Dage-MTI, IR2000) with a 40× objective (Nikon, 0.8 NA). The whole-cell recording was first formed to measure the baseline electrical properties (baseline RMP and so on). Neurons with access resistance larger than 30 MΩ or leak current larger than 300 pA (at −75 mV voltage clamp) were discarded. A small positive pressure (~0.5 psi) was maintained at the DNA tile-carrying pipette before contacting the neurona

### Preparation of giant vesicles
GUVs were prepared using an inverted emulsion method 78 . In brief, 1,2-dimyristoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (DMPC) and biotinylated lipids were mixed at a 1,000:1 molar ratio in chloroform in a glass vial. The solvent was evaporated under vacuum for 30 min to form a dry lipid film, which was subsequently resuspended in 600 μl of mineral oil and sealed with Parafilm. The oil–lipid suspension was sonicated at 50 °C for approximately 3 h to ensure homogeneous lipid dispersion.
Aqueous droplets were generated by adding 20 μl of Tris buffer (40 mM Tris, 1 mM EDTA, 20 mM acetic acid, pH 8.0) to the oil–lipid mixture, followed by vortexing for 30 s to produce a cloudy emulsion consisting of lipid-coated water droplets. A total of 600 μl of the emulsion was gently layered onto 300 μl of the same Tris buffer to establish an oil–water interface. The sample was centrifuged at 8,000 × g for 15 min, during which monolayer-coated droplets crossed the interface and assembled into bilayered GUVs that accumulated in the aqueous phase. After centrifugation, the mineral oil supernatant was carefully removed, and the GUVs were collected from the buffer phase.

### Microfluidic channel assembly
Microfluidic channels were fabricated by sealing a thin glass coverslip to a quartz slide using medical-grade acrylic double-sided adhesive tape. The channel geometry was defined by patterned slots cut into the adhesive layer. Before assembly, the glass coverslip was treated with piranha solution (H 2 SO 4 (3%):H 2 O 2 (1%)) to render the surface hydrophilic.

### GUV imaging
GUVs were imaged using a custom-built inverted fluorescence microscope based on a Zeiss Axio Observer D1 platform. Excitation was provided by diode lasers at 561 nm and 658 nm (Laserglow Technologies). Fluorescence emission was collected through a 63× oil-immersion objective (Zeiss) and detected with an Andor iXon3 electron-multiplying charge-coupled device camera.

### Abstract
Transmembrane ionic flow through artificial ion channels is integral to the development of biohybrid electronics, such as neural interface technologies. However, achieving accurate and stable intracellular access through these synthetic analogues has remained a challenge. Here we use DNA origami tiles (0.8 nm diameter), anchored into live neuronal membranes, both with and without cholesterol tags, to demonstrate highly stable ion transport (net ~2 nS), channel-like stochasticity and intracellular drug delivery without disrupting neuronal physiology. These results are supported by molecular dynamics simulations. Using a suite of patch-clamp techniques, including two-photon-targeted variants, we obtain repeatable intracellular and quasi-intracellular voltage measurements across DNA tiles, eliminating the need for membrane break-in even from thin dendritic structures (~1 µm), which are inaccessible with standard electrodes. This advancement establishes an ‘outside looking in’ method to probe intracellular voltage dynamics using DNA nanostructure-based transmembrane access.
Subject terms: Nanostructures, Characterization and analytical techniques, Drug delivery

### Main
Precise measurement of ionic flow across cellular membranes is fundamental when assaying bioelectricity in intact cells 1 . Traditional methods, such as whole-cell patch-clamp techniques 2 , offer invaluable insights into cellular dynamics but face major limitations, particularly when accessing smaller, more complex cellular structures or achieving stable intracellular measurements without disrupting integrity 3 . Recent bioengineering advances aim to overcome these challenges through innovations such as genetically encoded light and voltage-sensitive reporters 4 , synthetic analogues of ion channels such as carbon tiles 5 , 6 , and novel nanostructures 7 . However, achieving stable, repeatable electrical recordings with these tools remains difficult.
Artificial nanostructures—such as nanopipettes 8 , carbon nanotubes 5 , 9 , three-dimensional (3D) nanoelectrodes 10 – 12 and nanowires 13 , 14 —show promise as minimally invasive intracellular interfaces for neuronal recording 15 . Unlike traditional electrodes that often cause tissue damage, these nanoelectrodes minimally penetrate membranes, detecting subthreshold potentials, action potentials and previously inaccessible synaptic activity 16 – 19 . Yet intracellular recording still requires membrane rupture, which can disrupt physiology. Surface modifications and newer approaches to membrane access may help mitigate this issue 20 . Thus, novel nanostructures capable of self-insertion and lipid bilayer remodelling are needed to achieve seamless electrical access. Neurons rely on transmembrane ion flow for signalling 21 , and synthetically replicating this through artificial channels requires lipid bilayer membrane remodelling 22 . A promising approach uses artificial DNA tiles 23 , offering a platform for mimicking natural ion channel function. These biocompatible, ion-permissive nanostructures 24 – 26 enable transmembrane ionic transport, biosensing and membrane alteration 27 , 28 . Further modifications with hydrop

### DNA tiles enable ionic current measurements across neuronal membranes
The DNA tile assemblies feature tunable length 41 and channel size 42 , 43 . As previously reported 37 , each tile comprises 11-nm-long DNA duplexes with a 0.8 nm central cavity (Fig. 1a ). Eight single strands assemble into four duplexes; two include cholesterol molecules to facilitate membrane interfacing and two carry Cy3 or Alexa 488 for two-photon imaging. DNA sequences and chemical modifications are listed in Supplementary Table 1 , and their alignment with two-dimensional (2D) duplex maps is shown in Supplementary Fig. 1 .

### DNA tiles enable molecular delivery across neuronal membranes
Using dual-patch current-clamp recordings, we demonstrate that embedded DNA tiles enable intracellular delivery of small molecules, confirming transmembrane transport (Fig. 2 ). To validate this, we tested the transfer of a water-soluble, membrane-impermeable Alexa Fluor dye (~500 g mol −1 , negatively charged). Compared with capped tiles and control buffer, DNA tiles facilitated dye entry into neurons (Supplementary Fig. 10 ), confirming targeted molecular transport across membrane-anchored tiles.

### Characterization of pore resistance in neuronal membranes
The voltage-clamp recordings in Fig. 1 established DNA tile insertion into neuronal membranes via conductance changes but did not allow precise estimation of pore resistance owing to circuit constraints (Supplementary Note 1 ). To refine these measurements, we used a dual-pipette configuration ( Methods and Fig. 3a ). Two-photon imaging confirmed that tiles remained confined to the membrane patch in the cell-attached pipette, with no fluorescence wash-in, indicating that membrane integrity was preserved (Fig. 3b ). We analytically solved the equivalent circuit of the dual recording before and after tile insertion (Fig. 3c and Supplementary Fig. 13a ). Before insertion, the pipette voltage ( V p ) was dominated by the membrane capacitance (Fig. 3c(i) ), acting as a high-pass filter of the membrane voltage ( V m ) 46 . Upon tile insertion, ion permeability introduced a finite pore resistance ( R pore ), which became the dominant element so that V p tracked a linearly scaled V m (Fig. 3c(ii) ). Circuit simulations (Supplementary Note 1 ) predicted that, as tiles insert, steady-state V p decreases while whole-cell voltage ( V w ) increases (Fig. 3d ), consistent with experimental recordings (Fig. 3e ). These simulations further indicated that R pore can be reliably estimated up to several GΩ (Supplementary Fig. 13 ), within the range observed when tiles insert (Fig. 1g ). Using the dual-pipette approach, we obtained pore resistances of 542 ± 231 MΩ ( n = 13 neurons), in good agreement with the coarse estimate from Fig. 1g .

### Fig. 3. Estimation of tile resistance.
a , Schematic of the dual-pipette experimental set-up in which one pipette is loaded with DNA tiles and sealed to the cell membrane (black), while a second pipette is loaded with intracellular solution performing a conventional whole-cell patch-clamp recording (red). b , A two-photon image of the dual-patch set-up described in a . Scale bar, 20 µm. c , Equivalent circuit diagram describing the interface between the cell-attached pipette before (i) and after (ii) tile insertion. Upon insertion, the recorded pipette voltage ( V p ) will change from an extracellular capacitive-filtered waveform to a linearly scaled one (quasi-intracellular recording). d , Numerical simulation of steady-state cell-attached (blue) and whole-cell (red) voltages as a function of pore resistance. R seal = 75 MΩ, C m = 60 pF, R m = 55.6 MΩ. e , Evolution of voltage recordings from the whole-cell and cell-attached electrodes during the tile insertion. f , (i) No change in neuron input resistance (left) and intracellular Ca 2+ level (right) before (black) and after (red) tile insertion (two-sided paired-sample t -test, R in , n = 11 neurons; Ca 2+ level, n = 9 neurons). ### Quasi-intracellular access through DNA tiles
DNA tiles that form nanopore-like access across neuronal membranes should, in principle, support the same recording modes as nanoelectrode interfaces, including quasi-intracellular recordings analogous to nanopipettes 16 (Fig. 4a ). Numerical simulations supported this idea: as pore resistance decreased, the action potential (AP) recorded through the tile–membrane interface transitioned from a capacitively filtered extracellular waveform to a scaled intracellular waveform with increased amplitude (Supplementary Fig. 17 and Supplementary Note 2 ).

The centre and the bounds of the box plots represent 50%, 25% and 75% percentiles, and the whiskers represent 1.5 interquartile range below/above the first or the third quartile. d , DNA tiles facilitate stable repeatable cell-attached quasi-intracellular measures.
